extracted.intended_audience: reporters, editors, and newsroom staff covering trans people and trans-related topics
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style and coverage guide for reporting on transgender, nonbinary, and gender-diverse people and related issues, covering language, sourcing, visuals, topical beats, and sensitive editorial judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: self-identification is paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to determine a person's gender, name, and pronouns is to ask them directly; public records, police reports, family statements, and social media can be wrong or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take extra care in breaking news where misidentification is common. Use self-identification whenever safe and practicable; do not rely on secondary sources. Ask all sources for pronouns when safe and practical, and treat self-ID as the primary source of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'trans issues' is a euphemism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid collapsing varied laws, policies, and rhetoric into the shorthand 'trans issues'; the phrase obscures specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about what is at stake (civil rights protections, health care access, identity documents, etc.). Use precise language to lay out the stakes and avoid vague euphemisms that erase policy distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: talk to trans people about trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on issues affecting trans communities, interview trans people with relevant knowledge, experience, or expertise and center their voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include trans people as primary sources rather than treating them only as subjects. Researchers who study trans communities may also be trans themselves; prioritize relevant lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: talk to trans people about things besides trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: Include trans people as sources across beats for subjects unrelated to gender, recognizing gender identity is only part of someone's identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a gender-diverse source pool for stronger reporting across topics. Do not limit trans sources to only trans-related stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: take care not to ask irrelevant or unnecessary questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asking trans people medical, sexual, or other private questions unless they are directly relevant to a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask only questions that are clearly relevant; follow less-extractive reporting practices (see 'Why Should I Tell You?'). Avoid salacious or invasive questioning about medical history or transition unless essential and on-the-record with informed consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: never out sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not disclose someone’s trans status without their explicit permission; clarify implications of being identified as trans in published work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some people are out only in limited contexts; ensure they understand the risks of being identified and confirm what is on/off the record. Treat outing as a serious ethical breach with safety implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: there is no single 'trans community'
rubrics_metrics.description: Trans people are diverse across race, ethnicity, age, ability, nationality, political belief, religion, tribal membership, economic background, and more; do not treat one person's experience as representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek diverse sources to reflect different perspectives within trans communities; avoid essentializing or flattening complex differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: trans terms and identities vary across cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all languages or cultures have direct equivalents for 'transgender'; terms and meanings vary and may not map onto English categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult experts and community members when reporting cross-culturally. Avoid simplistic translations (e.g., travesti ≠ automatically 'transgender woman') and provide culturally specific context when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: be aware of slurs and other inflammatory language
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow industry guidance when reprinting slurs or inflammatory terms — generally only in direct quotes and only when necessary for comprehension, with editorial approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AP or newsroom policy on slur reprinting; most quotations will not meet the bar. Flag inflammatory language for additional editorial consideration; consider inline fact-checks for claims invoking misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: consult broader industry best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use other beat- and topic-specific guidance in addition to this stylebook (health, trauma reporting, education, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant, consult Association of Health Care Journalists, Dart Center for Trauma, Education Writers Association, and other specialized guides referenced in this stylebook for deeper technical or ethical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: don’t guess anyone’s gender identity or pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer a person's gender identity or pronouns from appearance, name, or other signals; ask when safe and practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it routine to ask all sources for pronouns when appropriate; be particularly careful in stories likely to involve LGBTQ+ people. See self-identification guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: do not call unnecessary attention to a trans person's gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Only identify someone as transgender when it provides necessary and relevant context; avoid making trans status the focal point when it is not pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters rarely note cisgender people’s genders; apply the same restraint to trans people. Be concise when defining common terms like 'nonbinary' and avoid unnecessary explanations for familiar audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: writing about someone in the past — use current name and pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a person’s current name and pronouns when referring to their past unless they request otherwise; omit or bracket deadnaming/misgendering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trans person requests to quote their own past deadnaming/misgendering, publish verbatim only if it adds clear value and was expressly consented to. For deadnaming/misgendering by others, bracket or paraphrase and make clear the inaccuracy if helpful for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'identifies as' just means 'is'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrasing like 'identifies as a man' or 'identifies as nonbinary' for trans or non-trans people; state the identity plainly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'is a man', 'is nonbinary', etc., without the qualifying phrase 'identifies as' unless directly quoting someone using that language.

rubrics_metrics.name: deadnames — never publish without permission
rubrics_metrics.description: A deadname is a name a trans person no longer uses; do not publish it without express permission as it can be offensive and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-profile cases may be complex but still require sensitivity; do not proactively update published stories unless (1) the original identification was incorrect at publication (issue correction) or (2) the person who was identified correctly has since changed identity and requested retroactive update (honor per newsroom standards). Update web assets (tags, alt text, redirects) where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: when sources or past coverage deadname/misgender
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting someone who deadnames or misgenders, do not publish those portions verbatim; bracket or paraphrase and note they were being deadnamed/misgendered if useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In print, use brackets to correct or paraphrase; be mindful with multimedia and visual media guidance for similar adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: pronoun basics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask sources what pronouns they want published and respect that choice; use pronouns normally in copy rather than attempting to avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid circumlocutions to dodge pronoun use. There is generally no need to explain common pronouns in copy; explain only in contexts where prior misstatements or clarity make it helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender-neutral pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use they/them and other gender-neutral pronouns (ze/hir, ey/em, etc.) appropriately and accurately as provided by sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect neopronouns and consult sources for spelling and usage. Use newsroom references on neopronoun history/grammar when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: multiple pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people use more than one set of pronouns (e.g., he/they); ask which pronouns they want published and follow their preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be appropriate to explain multiple pronoun usage in context; there are examples of published stories that use multiple pronouns with or without explanation. Use editorial judgment on clarity and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: neopronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Neopronouns are third-person singular pronouns other than they/them (e.g., ze/hir, xe/xer); do not substitute they/them automatically and ask for correct spelling/usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure of spelling or usage, ask the person. Recognize variations between similar-sounding neopronouns and use them correctly if requested for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: preferred pronouns — avoid the phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the phrase 'preferred pronouns' as pronouns are not a preference but how someone must be referred to; use 'pronouns' unless someone uses multiple sets and expresses a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'preferred pronouns' for situations where an individual indicates multiple acceptable pronoun sets and has a preference among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: singular they/them pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular they is widely accepted and should be used when appropriate; it takes plural verb agreement and can use 'themself' or 'themselves' (themself preferred for clarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no need to explain usage of standard singular they in most stories. Avoid treating singular they as unique to trans people; use it when a person's pronouns warrant it.

rubrics_metrics.name: what to do if you can’t determine someone’s pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not avoid names or pronouns simply because someone is trans or nonbinary; write around pronouns only when it is impossible to determine them safely or accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some outlets use singular they as a default for unknown persons; others prefer writing around pronouns. Choose per newsroom style, but avoid erasing or misgendering people by omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: assigned sex at birth — use precise phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'assigned sex at birth' rather than 'born female'/'born a girl'; the phrase clarifies that sex labels are assigned by others at birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigned sex generally refers to anatomy; assigned gender may be used when appropriate. Use AMAB/AFAB when relevant but do not apply these labels to individuals who do not use them. Provide nuance about intersex and avoid using these labels as nouns (e.g., 'an AFAB').

rubrics_metrics.name: biological sex — use cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'biological sex' as a synonym for assigned sex at birth outside medical literature because it is politicized and ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering policy, quote legal definitions directly and explain how a given law defines 'biological sex.' Avoid uncritically reprinting speculation about an individual's 'biological sex'; such rumors are often inaccurate and may create legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: culture war — use sparingly and specifically
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve 'culture war' for sweeping references; avoid using it as a euphemism for LGBTQ+/trans policy debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the actual debate or policy rather than using 'culture war' as shorthand; fact-check claims about prevalence and content of culture-war narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: detransitioner — avoid as label unless quoting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'detransitioner' as a descriptor unless in direct quotes; some who stop transition find the label offensive or inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the person's actions (stopped hormones, changed legal status) and avoid blanket labels or assumptions about motives without reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender ideology — avoid loaded phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the charged phrase 'gender ideology' deployed by anti-trans actors; instead use neutral descriptors like 'trans identity' or 'being transgender.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'gender ideology' from 'gender-critical' perspectives when relevant and provide context rather than repeating activist language uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender nonbinary — grammatically incorrect phrasing to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the phrase 'gender nonbinary' (e.g., 'gender nonbinary person'); use 'nonbinary' as an adjective or 'nonbinary person' directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same conventions as for 'woman' or 'man' when referring to gender labels; keep definitions concise and audience-appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: groomer/grooming — treat as a serious accusation
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations of grooming connote child sexual abuse and must be treated with corresponding seriousness and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quoting someone who uses the term, make clear whether they allege proven abuse or are using rhetoric. Avoid repeating 'groomer' as an insult without context; false claims can be defamatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: male-bodied/female-bodied — avoid reductive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'male-bodied' and 'female-bodied' terms as reductive and often deployed pejoratively regarding assigned sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more precise phrasing about anatomy or assigned sex if medically relevant; avoid language that reduces people to body parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: mutilation/sterilization — avoid inflammatory rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeating opponents' loaded terms like 'mutilation' or 'sterilization' for transition-related care without fact-checking and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-check claims about fertility impacts and avoid amplifying misinformation about youth care; provide medical and policy context when such claims appear in public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: opposite sex/opposite gender — avoid binary framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrasing that positions men/males and women/females as opposites; it reinforces an inaccurate gender binary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that acknowledges difference without casting genders as oppositional; prefer precise descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: rapid-onset gender dysphoria/social contagion — treat as discredited
rubrics_metrics.description: The rapid-onset gender dysphoria/social contagion theory has been extensively corrected and discredited; be clear about the lack of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quoting claims about it, note the scientific consensus and corrections to the original studies; avoid amplifying debunked theories without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: stealth/passing — avoid judging or asserting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not describe someone as 'stealth' or assess whether they 'pass' based on reporter observation; those terms are community-specific and sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on passing or stealth only when relevant and usually as quoted language from the person themself; avoid making reporter judgments about appearance-based passing.

rubrics_metrics.name: transgenderism/trans ideology/trans agenda — avoid loaded terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use '-ism' phrasing that casts trans identity as a political philosophy; prefer neutral terms like 'transness' or 'transgender identity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name specific actors, policies, or beliefs rather than repeating pejorative umbrella terms. Use 'anti-trans' modifiers for rhetoric or policies that oppose trans inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: transgendered — outdated term; do not use
rubrics_metrics.description: The form 'transgendered' is outdated and generally offensive—use 'transgender' or 'trans' as an adjective instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'transgendered' outside direct quotation; use 'transgender person' or simply 'trans person.'

rubrics_metrics.name: trans activists/trans rights activists — be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate existing as a trans person with being an activist; identify people as activists only if they engage in activism or self-identify that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more specific descriptors (trans health care advocates, supporters of trans athletes) and avoid blanket labels that imply political motives by mere existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: TERF / trans-exclusionary radical feminist — explain and use carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: TERF refers to an ideology that denies trans identities; the term can be pejorative and should be used only with context or when the subject uses it themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessary to report, define the term and provide context rather than using it as an interchangeable label; consider using 'anti-trans' as a neutral modifier for ideas or policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: breaking news — identifying transgender people
rubrics_metrics.description: In breaking news, extra caution is required before identifying someone as transgender because initial reports commonly misidentify people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize self-identification, corroboration, and safety. If you cannot obtain self-identification, follow the breaking-news topical guidance on writing around uncertain gender and protecting sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: what to do if you can’t obtain self-identification (breaking news)
rubrics_metrics.description: When self-identification is unavailable in urgent reporting, use cautious practices to avoid misidentification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write around gender when possible, avoid speculative language, explain uncertainty to readers, and consult the breaking-news guidance for best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: practicing trauma-informed reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trauma-informed approaches when reporting on distressing events that affect trans people, especially victims of violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the Dart Center guidance and other referenced resources for interviewing trauma-affected sources, protecting mental health, and avoiding re-traumatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: publishing identifying information about trans children
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise heightened caution and consult education- and child-focused reporting guidance before publishing identifying details about trans minors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Education Writers Association and newsroom policies; get informed consent, consider safety and legal implications, and avoid unnecessary disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: reporting on the deaths of trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: Report with sensitivity and accuracy when covering the deaths of trans people, recognizing higher risk of violence and community impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sensationalism, verify identity with care, respect family wishes when possible, and highlight context about anti-trans violence rather than speculative motive attribution without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: general guidance on reporting anti-trans laws and policies
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering anti-trans legislation or policy, explain definitions used by laws, and focus on practical effects rather than purely legalistic jargon for general audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote legal language directly when necessary, explain differences across jurisdictions, and describe tangible impacts (e.g., bans restricting health care, bathroom restrictions) for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: reporting on U.S. trans health care bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise language and medical context when covering health-care restrictions affecting trans people; avoid amplifying misinformation about medical procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult health-care reporting guides, explain what services are actually affected (e.g., puberty blockers vs surgery), and include medical expert context about effects and rarity of procedures in minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: reporting on nondiscrimination laws related to trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering nondiscrimination protections, clarify statutory language (sex-based vs gender-based) and how courts have interpreted protections for trans people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain legal terms, note jurisdictional differences, and focus on real-world consequences of policy language for trans individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: criminal justice reporting: avoid anti-trans misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to anti-trans misinformation in coverage of mass shootings and extremist activities; verify and contextualize claims linking trans people to violent acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat baseless claims; provide evidence and expert analysis when allegations involve gender identity, and consider how carceral policy and gender identity interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: reporting on incarcerated trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on incarcerated trans people with attention to safety, identity, and the interaction of carceral policy with gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider privacy risks, consult policy experts, avoid inadvertent outing, and be careful when identifying sources in prisons or jails.

rubrics_metrics.name: language around transgender health care
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accurate, non-stigmatizing language to describe gender-affirming care and related medical services; prefer technical clarity over politicized rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'gender-affirming care', 'transgender medical care', or similarly precise terms. Avoid inflammatory or caricaturing language; provide medical context and expert perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: consider whether protected health information is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publishing medical or health information about a trans person, assess whether it is necessary to the story and consider privacy and safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing protected health information unless it is essential and the subject has given informed permission. Follow applicable legal/ethical standards for health privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: detransition/retransition coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover people who stop or restart transition carefully without generalizing; do not use labels like 'detransitioner' without context and avoid assuming motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report individual circumstances with nuance, avoid treating their stories as proof of broader trends, and consult medical and sociological context where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: reporting on trans people in sports
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise terms and avoid treating 'transgender athletes' as a monolith; explain policy details and physiological questions with evidence and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify what regulations govern eligibility (testosterone rules, sex-designated categories), discuss competitive advantage questions with experts, and treat youth-sports debates as distinct from adult competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: describing how trans people look
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid speculative or stereotyped descriptions of appearance; use respectful, necessary details and center consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on appearance to assert someone’s gender; use descriptions that are relevant to the story and avoid objectifying or sensationalized language.

rubrics_metrics.name: other topical guidance (drag, obituaries, asylum, sex work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context-specific guidance for beats like drag culture, obituaries, asylum seekers, sex work, same-sex marriage, and reporting clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the dedicated subsections for each topic (e.g., obituaries: avoid deadnaming; asylum: provide cultural and legal context), and consult beat experts and community sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: photography and visual media: protect sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid images or metadata that could endanger subjects; obtain informed consent and ensure visuals do not deadname or misgender people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or correct deadnames in file metadata, use file photos with care, avoid inappropriate stock images, and follow consent best practices for vulnerable subjects. Obscure identifying information when necessary for safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: gender-affirming care
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-affirming care includes counseling, puberty blockers, hormones, procedures like electrolysis or surgery, and other medical or social steps people pursue as part of transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term as a technical descriptor; when needed, specify particular treatments rather than relying on broad euphemisms. Recognize different connotations across audiences and legal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: gender dysphoria and gender euphoria
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender dysphoria refers to distress some people feel when their bodies or social treatment don't align with their gender; gender euphoria refers to comfort and happiness when gender is affirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that not all trans people experience dysphoria; provide context when using these terms and avoid pathologizing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: nonbinary
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonbinary is an umbrella term for genders other than man and woman; not all nonbinary people consider themselves trans and do not automatically equate to 'trans'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically identify someone as trans simply because they are nonbinary; use the terms the person uses for themself.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: intersex
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone born with reproductive anatomy, chromosomes, or hormones that do not fit strict binary understandings of male/female; intersex people can be any gender and may or may not identify as trans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'intersex' as a noun referring to a person without their consent; consult InterACT and other resources for reporting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: trans, transgender, transness
rubrics_metrics.description: Trans (short for transgender) is an adjective describing someone whose gender is not—or not exclusively—the one assigned at birth; 'transness' is a neutral noun describing the attribute of being transgender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'trans' as an adjective (trans woman, trans man). Do not use 'transgender' as a noun or apply '-ism' phrasing that politicizes identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: trans woman / trans man / transmasculine / transfeminine
rubrics_metrics.description: A trans woman is a woman who is trans; a trans man is a man who is trans. Transfeminine/transmasculine are descriptive umbrella terms for gendered experiences oriented toward femininity/masculinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-word constructions (trans woman, trans man). Prefer 'trans women' over 'transfeminine people' when referring specifically to trans women, and avoid intracommunity slang as news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: misgender / misgendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Misgendering is using gendered words or pronouns inappropriate for someone, whether intentional or accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misgendering sources; correct errors promptly and transparently when they occur. When reporting others' misgendering, make clear it was a misgendering if that context is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: deadname
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadname is a name someone no longer uses; publishing it without permission can be offensive and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never publish a deadname without express permission. Remove deadnames from backend assets when feasible and honor update requests per newsroom policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: transition (social, medical, legal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition encompasses social, medical, and legal steps someone may take to align life with their gender: name/pronoun change, dress, medical care, and document changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize transition as potentially partial or ongoing, and be precise about which aspects are relevant to the story rather than assuming a single pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: transmisogyny / transmisogynoir
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmisogyny is the unique oppression transfeminine people face due to both misogyny and transphobia; transmisogynoir specifically references the combined impacts of racism, misogyny, and transphobia experienced by Black trans women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these terms when describing intersectional harms with appropriate attribution and explanation for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: glossary: Two-Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-Spirit is an Indigenous term encompassing identity and spirituality, always capitalized, with context-specific meanings that vary by tribal nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an Indigenous person uses Two-Spirit, ask how they define it and include tribal or national identity context; standardize spelling outside verbatim quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: use precise legal language only when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: In legal reporting, use jurisdiction-specific technical language; outside legal reporting, prefer plain language focused on tangible effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote statutory language when necessary and explain how definitions might vary across jurisdictions. For general audiences, describe the real-world implications rather than legalese alone.
